why: LCA made simple by the ordering: walk down from the root; while both values are smaller go left, while both are larger go right; the first node that separates them (or equals one) is the LCA.
hints: At the root, if p and q are both smaller than it, where must their LCA be?
If both are smaller go left, if both are larger go right; otherwise the current node lies between them (or equals one of them) and is the answer.
A single loop from the root, no recursion and no extra storage: O(h) time, O(1) space.
pitfalls: A node is its own ancestor: if p is an ancestor of q, the answer is p.
p and q may be equal; the answer is then that node.
Compare against min(p, q) and max(p, q), not p and q in the given order.
